# Bhikkhu Pātimokkha (Pm Bu)

**ID:** Pm Bu
**Section:** Pātimokkha (pm)
**Collection:** Vinaya
**Title (Pali):** Bhikkhu Pātimokkha
**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** The Monks’ Rules
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/pli-tv-bu-pm

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Bhikkhu Pātimokkha* ("The Monks' Rules") is the foundational disciplinary code governing the Buddhist monastic order for monks, preserved in the Vinaya Piṭaka [SuttaCentral]. It comprises an unannotated list of 227 monastic training rules (*sikkhāpada*), organized according to the gravity of the offense incurred for transgressing them [SuttaCentral; Norman 1983; Blackstone 1995]. These divisions include the *pārājika* rules (which entail immediate and irrevocable expulsion from the Saṅgha, the first being the prohibition against sexual intercourse), *saṅghādisesa*, *nissaggiya pācittiya*, and *pācittiya*, alongside non-punitive procedural frameworks: the *aniyatas* ("undetermined") and the *adhikaraṇasamathadhammas* ("principles for resolving legal issues") [SuttaCentral; Sujato 2009; Blackstone 1995]. Although transmitted in the canon embedded within the explanatory stories and analyses of the *Suttavibhaṅga*, the text originally existed as an independent recitation piece known as the *Pātimokkha-sutta*, as evinced by sequential cross-references between rules that the intervening Vibhaṅga material now separates [SuttaCentral]. In early commentary, the Porāṇas also referred to the *Anumāna Sutta* of the Majjhima Nikāya by the designation *Bhikkhupātimokkha* [Adikaram 1946; Prebish 2002].

The traditional commentary *Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī* systematically expounds all 227 rules according to a standard schema: grammatical parsing of the rule, juridical determination of offenses, mitigating circumstances, exceptions incurring guiltlessness, and hermeneutic summaries [Norman 1983]. Individual rules regulate monastic deportment, robe usage, relations with unordained persons (*anupasampanna*), and textual instruction, such as *pācittiya* 4 forbidding teaching the Dhamma "word-by-word" (*padaso*) to non-ordained individuals [Clarke; Sujato 2009; Wynne 2007].

The most severe categories of the code (*pārājika*, *saṅghādisesa*, *aniyata*, and *pācittiya*) show remarkable agreement in number and substance across the Vinayas of different Buddhist schools [Blackstone 1995]. DharmaNexus identifies extensive cross-language alignments with Sanskrit *Prātimokṣasūtra* texts of the Mahāsāṅghika and Mūlasarvāstivādin traditions (such as SA_K01_prmosubu, scoring up to 95), Tibetan translations of the *Bhikṣuṇīprātimokṣasūtra* (D0004), the *Vinayasūtra*, and commentaries like the *Pratimokṣasūtrapaddhati* [DharmaNexus; Prebish 2002]. Internally, DharmaNexus records 7,989 matching passages across 239 Pali texts, with the largest text-reuse shares occurring in the *Bhikkhunī Pātimokkha*, the *Suttavibhaṅga*, the *Parivāra* (such as the *Katthapaññattivāra* and *Katāpattivāra*), and post-canonical handbooks like the *Khuddasikkhā* [DharmaNexus; Norman 1983]. Major English translations include those by T. W. Rhys Davids and Hermann Oldenberg, and by Bhikkhu Brahmali [Rhys Davids & Oldenberg 1881; SuttaCentral].
